beats.text: Each map holds five hundred thirty-seven bomb hits. On one, every hit landed by pure chance. The other follows a rule. Which one is chance? [pause 1.5]
Both are simulated. The question isn't. In nineteen forty-four, Londoners claimed German flying bombs fell in clusters, and precise aim would put factories at risk.
Build the detector your eye is running. Cut each map into five hundred seventy-six squares, count the hits, and flag any square with three or more, like this one.
Map A lights up with thirty-nine targets. Map B gets none. So A looks aimed.

Backwards. [pause 0.9] I dropped every hit on map A at random, so all thirty-nine targets are false alarms. Map B's rule: no two hits closer than four fifths of a square. The detector, like your eye, expected chance to spread out that evenly.
Take one square. Each bomb has a one in five hundred seventy-six chance of landing in it. To stay empty, all five hundred thirty-seven must miss.
Guess how many squares get no hit at all. [pause 1.5]
About two hundred twenty-seven squares stay empty. Map A has two hundred twenty-two.
Those empty squares force the clumps: the other three hundred fifty-four squares share all the hits, one and a half each, so plenty must double up. To judge London, chance must predict every bar.
Call the average hits per square lambda. [pause 0.5] One minus a small slice, raised to a big power, is almost exactly e to the minus lambda. [pause 0.5]

For two hits, pick which two bombs land here: five thirty-seven times five thirty-six ways, over two, since order doesn't matter. [pause 0.4] Each lands with chance one in five seventy-six, and the rest miss: e to the minus lambda again. [pause 0.4]

Five thirty-six is almost five thirty-seven. [pause 0.4] For three hits, each two becomes a three; for any k, a k. [pause 0.6] The powers merge into lambda to the k: the Poisson distribution. [pause 0.7] Times five hundred seventy-six squares, it predicts these purple bars.

The honest detector compares whole histograms. [pause 0.8] Thirty-nine targets, and chance predicts thirty-nine. The chi-squared misfit: square each bar's gap and divide by chance's bar, so a miss of two on seven outweighs a miss of five on two hundred twenty-seven. Add them up: map A scores two point oh. Three in four simulated chance maps score worse. [pause 0.3] That share, p, is point seven four.
Map B: half the expected empty squares, a tower of single hits, and a misfit of two hundred seventy-two. A pattern this even is the fingerprint of a spacing rule.

Aimed bombs would miss the other way: extra empty squares, extra pile-ups. In nineteen forty-six, the actuary R D Clarke published this test on real flying-bomb hits: five hundred thirty-seven, in five hundred seventy-six squares of London.

Chance predicted two hundred twenty-seven empty squares; Clarke counted two hundred twenty-nine. [pause 0.2] Single hits: two hundred eleven, exactly as predicted. [pause 0.2] Same test: p equals point eight eight.

The bombs were aimed at Tower Bridge, but half fell more than twelve kilometres away, outside this circle and off this map. And the test needs one lambda everywhere: farther north, hits were about half as dense, so Clarke chose an area where lambda held steady.
So look again. [pause 1.2] The clumps in map A are what no aim at all looks like. If you chose map B, you chose the one following a rule.
